q: Identify the threshold stimulus.
Between 2 and 3 units.
Explain why every action potential peaked at +30 mV.
Action potentials are all-or-nothing: once threshold is reached, voltage-gated sodium channels open fully, so each one is the same size.
Explain how the neuron tells the brain the difference between stimuli of 4 and 8 units.
By the frequency of impulses: about 30 per second at 4 units and 130 at 8 units.
Explain why the curve levels off near 180 impulses per second.
After each action potential there is a refractory period (sodium channels inactivated, potassium channels open) when a new one cannot start, which sets a maximum frequency.
Calculate the shortest time between impulses at stimulus 12.
Suggest how a strong stimulus can also be signalled without a higher frequency.
More sensory neurons are activated: receptors have different thresholds, so a strong stimulus recruits more of them.

18.t: Working with data: conduction speed and myelin damage
q: Calculate the time for an impulse to travel 0.8 m in a healthy nerve.
Calculate the percentage decrease in mean speed in severe MS.
Explain why damage to the myelin sheath slows conduction.
Where myelin is lost, ions leak and the membrane must be depolarised all along the damaged region, not just at the nodes: no saltatory conduction. Some impulses fade out completely.
The standard deviation is largest in the severe group. Suggest why.
The damage is patchy: it varies between patients and between nerves, so speeds vary more.

23.t: Working with data: a general anaesthetic
q: Describe the effect of the anaesthetic on IPSPs and EPSPs.
IPSPs become 2.4 times larger (-5 to -12 mV); EPSPs are unchanged.
Explain why the anaesthetic reduces the number of impulses.
The larger inhibitory potentials cancel out the excitatory ones during summation, so the membrane rarely reaches threshold.
Use the third column to deduce how the anaesthetic works.

When GABA receptors are blocked, the anaesthetic has no effect (IPSPs almost gone, firing high). So it works by making GABA receptors open more: more chloride ions enter and the neuron is hyperpolarised.
Explain why firing is higher than normal when GABA receptors are blocked.
Normal background inhibition is removed, so EPSPs reach threshold more often.
Suggest how fewer impulses could lead to loss of consciousness.
Consciousness is an emergent property of many neurons interacting; with fewer impulses, brain regions stop communicating.
